title: SELF JOIN
description: Join a table to itself to find hierarchical relationships and compare rows within the same table.

data.text: Sometimes a table references itself. An employee table has a manager_id that points back to another employee_id in the same table. To read that relationship, you join the table to itself — a SELF JOIN.
A self-join is just an INNER JOIN (or LEFT JOIN) where the same table appears twice in the FROM clause. You MUST give each occurrence a different alias, or SQL Server cannot tell them apart.

data.title: SELF JOIN skeleton
data.code:
SELECT e.col1, m.col2
FROM   employees e
INNER JOIN employees m
    ON m.employee_id = e.manager_id;

data.text: Every employee has a manager_id that references their manager's employee_id in the same table. The left alias (e) is the employee; the right alias (m) is the manager.

data.title: List every employee with their manager's name
data.code:
SELECT e.first_name  AS employee,
       e.last_name   AS emp_last,
       m.first_name  AS manager_first,
       m.last_name   AS manager_last
FROM   employees e
LEFT JOIN employees m
    ON m.employee_id = e.manager_id
ORDER BY e.last_name;

data.title: LEFT JOIN to include the top boss
data.text: If the CEO has a NULL manager_id, an INNER JOIN would exclude them. Use LEFT JOIN instead so every employee appears, with NULL in the manager columns for the top-level person.

items: Comparing rows within a table: find employees earning more than their own manager
Hierarchical chains: employee → manager → director (multi-level joins)
Sequential data: compare each row to the previous row by date or ID

data.title: Employees who earn more than their manager
data.code:
-- Assuming salaries table with employee_id and salary columns
SELECT e.first_name, e.last_name, e.salary
FROM   employees e
INNER JOIN employees m
    ON m.employee_id = e.manager_id
INNER JOIN salaries s1 ON s1.employee_id = e.employee_id
INNER JOIN salaries s2 ON s2.employee_id = m.employee_id
WHERE  s1.salary > s2.salary;

data.title: For deep hierarchies: recursive CTEs
data.text: If you need to traverse an unknown number of levels (e.g., a bill of materials with 10 layers), a SELF JOIN that manually chains N levels becomes unwieldy. The recursive CTE — covered in the next phase — is the better tool for arbitrary-depth hierarchies.

data.title: Self-join essentials
points: A self-join is a table joined to itself using different aliases
Aliases are mandatory — SQL Server cannot resolve two references to the same table name
LEFT JOIN keeps employees whose manager is NULL (e.g. the CEO)
Common use cases: org charts, sequential comparisons, finding anomalies
For arbitrary-depth hierarchies, prefer recursive CTEs over chained self-joins
